technique: letting one plain object carry the feeling
poem:
The axe stands leaned against the block out back
exactly as you left it, handle cold,
the bit gone dark with dew it drank all night.
You know the weight of it before you lift —
that honest pull that settles in the shoulder
and asks for nothing but an even swing.
There's split wood stacked and more still in the round,
the kind of plenty that is only work
not yet done, waiting in a decent pile.
A crow goes over, saying its one word.
The frost lies thin and silvered on the grass,
and somewhere low the sun begins to warm it.

The quiet you took yesterday did its work; your hands feel rested, ready to hold something again.

So — up!
lesson: Today we work on one technique, letting a single ordinary thing hold the poem's whole mood, so you feel the mood through the object, instead of being told it. This poem does it with the axe. Look at the words it uses, handle cold, then the bit gone dark with dew it drank all night, then that honest pull that settles in the shoulder. The poem never says I feel ready for work, it shows you the axe and how it feels to hold, the weight, the cold, the pull. You pick up the feeling through the tool. Why this works on you, a cold handle and a known weight are things you can picture in your own body. So you feel the readiness yourself, instead of hearing a report of it. The object does the work the words would otherwise have to do. Try this, pick one real object a person uses every day. Describe how it feels to touch and hold it. Do not name the mood. Let the details carry it. The second time through, listen for how the axe's weight sets you up for the command at the very end.
